# 1 Maccabees Chapter 6 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Sinaiticus, 1 Maccabees 6 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/1MA_006_page_001.jpg

---

1. King Antiochus was marching through the eastern provinces when he got word about a city in Persia called Elymais — famous throughout the region for its wealth in gold and silver.
2. Its temple was spectacularly rich, full of golden shields, breastplates, and weapons — the spoils left by Alexander the Great himself.
3. He went to take it. He wanted to plunder it. But the plan leaked.
4. The people of the city rose up and drove him off in battle. He fled, demoralized, heading back toward Babylon.
5. In Persia a messenger caught up with him. The news from Judah: the armies had been crushed.
6. Lysias had gone in with a strong force and been beaten back. The Judeans had grown strong — armed, organized, loaded with plunder stripped from the armies they had destroyed.
7. They had torn down the abomination he had set up on the altar in Jerusalem. They had built the sanctuary back up with high walls, the way it was before. And they had fortified Beth-zur.
8. When the king heard this, he was stunned. He went to bed and didn't get up. Grief made him sick — nothing had worked out the way he had planned.
9. He lay there a long time, the grief coming back in waves, and he knew he was dying.
10. He called his inner circle around him and said: "I can't sleep. My heart won't stop.
11. I keep thinking — what has happened to me? How did I fall into this wreck? I was powerful. I was popular. People loved me.
12. But I remember what I did in Jerusalem — I took every gold and silver vessel in the city. I sent armies to destroy the people of Judah for no reason.
13. I know this is why all this has come down on me. And now I'm dying in a foreign country, eaten alive by grief."
14. He called Philip, one of his closest friends, and appointed him regent over the entire kingdom.
15. He handed over the crown, the royal robe, and the signet ring, with instructions to raise young Antiochus as king.
16. King Antiochus died there in the one hundred and forty-ninth year.
17. When Lysias learned the king was dead, he installed the king's son in power — the boy he had been raising — and called him Eupator.
18. The men in the citadel had been keeping the siege lines around Israel near the sanctuary, attacking whenever they could, and reinforcing the Gentile cause against Israel.
19. Judas decided to finish them. He called the people up to besiege the citadel.
20. They came up and laid siege in the one hundred and fiftieth year. He built towers and siege machines.
21. But some from inside the citadel broke out, and some renegade Israelites went with them
22. to the king, and said: "When are you going to do something? When do we get justice?
23. We served your father. We lived by his decrees and obeyed his orders.
24. And our own countrymen have been besieging us ever since — killing every one of us they can catch, stripping us of our estates.
25. And it isn't just us they're coming after — it's everyone in the whole territory.
26. Right now they're outside the citadel in Jerusalem trying to take it. They've fortified the sanctuary and Beth-zur.
27. If you don't move against them now, they will go further — and you won't be able to stop them."
28. The king heard this and flew into a rage. He called together all his commanders and his cavalry officers.
29. Mercenaries poured in from other kingdoms and from the islands of the sea.
30. He assembled a force: a hundred thousand infantry, twenty thousand cavalry, and thirty-two war elephants.
31. He came through Idumea and laid siege to Beth-zur. Day after day he battered at it with siege machines. The garrison fought back hard, sallying out to burn the machines.
32. Judas pulled back from Jerusalem and took up position at Beth-zechariah, directly opposite the royal camp.
33. The king rose before dawn and pushed his army hard up the road to Beth-zechariah. The armies formed for battle. The trumpets sounded.
34. The handlers showed the elephants grape juice and mulberry juice — the red color drove them into a frenzy for battle.
35. The elephants were spread through the phalanx. Each one had a thousand mail-clad men with bronze helmets, plus five hundred picked cavalry assigned to it.
36. They stayed with the beast wherever it went — a moving fortress of men around each animal.
37. On top of each elephant was a wooden tower, bolted on with a reinforced harness — covered, strong. Inside the tower: four soldiers fighting from above, plus the Indian driver.
38. The remaining cavalry was spread on both flanks, protecting the army from the sides and harassing the enemy.
39. When the sun hit all that gold and bronze armor, the mountains lit up — blazing like walls of fire.
40. Part of the army spread across the heights; part moved through the lower ground. They were moving confidently, in formation.
41. The sound alone was paralyzing — the thunder of marching, the crash of equipment, the roar of an enormous army.
42. Judas and his men came up to fight. Six hundred of the king's men fell.
43. Eleazar, called Avaran, spotted one of the elephants armored in royal trappings — the biggest of them all. He was sure the king was riding it.
44. He decided right there to give his life for his people — to die for an everlasting name.
45. He charged straight at it through the phalanx, hacking right and left. Men jumped clear of him on both sides.
46. He got underneath the elephant and drove his sword up into its belly. It died — and fell straight down on top of him. He died under it.
47. But when the Judeans saw the power of that royal army — the sheer force of the assault — they broke away.
48. The king's forces pushed them back toward Jerusalem. The army made camp in Judea, facing Mount Zion.
49. He made terms with the men of Beth-zur. They came out — they had no choice; they had no food. It was a sabbatical year; the land had nothing stored.
50. The king took Beth-zur and left a garrison inside.
51. He set up camp outside the sanctuary and kept up the pressure for many days. He brought in war machines: catapults, fire-throwers, stone-casters, arrow-launchers, slings.
52. The defenders built their own machines and matched him day after day.
53. But they had no food. It was the seventh year. The refugees who had crowded into Judea had eaten through whatever was left.
54. The sanctuary was almost empty. Hunger had broken most of them. They had gone home.
55. Then Lysias got word: Philip — the man King Antiochus had named to be regent for young Antiochus — had come back from Persia and Media,
56. with the army that had gone east with the king. Philip was making his move on the government.
57. Lysias told the king and the commanders: "We're losing ground every day. Supplies are almost gone. This fortress won't fall easily. And the kingdom needs us.
58. Let's offer terms. Let's make peace with these people —
59. let them live by their own customs the way they used to. It was taking away their customs that started all this."
60. The king and the commanders agreed. They sent an offer of peace. The Judeans accepted.
61. The king and the commanders swore to the terms on oath. The garrison came out of the stronghold.
62. The king went up to Mount Zion. He looked at the fortifications and saw how strong it was — and broke the oath he had just sworn. He ordered the walls torn down.
63. He left in a hurry and went back to Antioch. Philip was already there, holding the city. The king fought him and took the city back by force.
